question: How is a nursing manager's decision different from the choices you make at a patient's bedside?

options.B: Treating one specific patient at a time
options.D: Affecting entire units, staff, and budgets

explanation: At the bedside, you focus on one patient at a time. But as a manager, your decisions ripple across the whole ward, affecting staff duties and hospital resources! [learn more](GST321_U1_T8#GST321_U1_T8_h1)

question: Why is it helpful for a new nurse manager to see their administrative duties as making active choices?

options.A: It removes the need to consult senior staff
options.B: It speeds up the process of writing shift reports
options.C: It helps them take responsibility for outcomes
options.D: It guarantees that no mistakes will ever happen

explanation: When you accept that leadership is all about making choices, you can own the results, learn quickly from mistakes, and grow into a confident leader. [learn more](GST321_U1_T8#GST321_U1_T8_h1)

question: What do we call the routine choices you make using already established hospital rules and procedures?
explanation: Programmed choices are your go-to solutions for familiar, everyday situations where a clear hospital guideline already exists. [learn more](GST321_U1_T8#GST321_U1_T8_h2)

question: Imagine a sudden disease outbreak hits your ward and there is no existing hospital policy for it. What type of choice must you make?
explanation: When a situation is totally new and unstructured, standard rules won't cut it. You have to make a non-programmed choice! [learn more](GST321_U1_T8#GST321_U1_T8_h2)

question: What is the very first step you should take in the decision-making process?
explanation: You can't fix what you haven't defined! Spotting the exact gap between your current challenge and your goal is always step one. [learn more](GST321_U1_T8#GST321_U1_T8_h3)

question: Why is it a good idea to brainstorm several different options before making a final management decision?

options.A: It ensures that every staff member gets promoted
options.B: It prevents settling prematurely on a poor solution
options.C: It makes the decision-making process instantaneous
options.D: It eliminates the need to evaluate costs

explanation: Looking at multiple alternatives stops you from jumping blindly at the very first idea that pops into your head. [learn more](GST321_U1_T8#GST321_U1_T8_h3)

question: What goes wrong when a manager only treats the surface symptoms of a ward problem?

options.A: Hospital management will immediately fire the nursing staff
options.B: The budget for the ward will be permanently frozen
options.C: The underlying issue remains and will happen again
options.D: Patients will stop coming to the clinic entirely

explanation: Just scratching the surface leaves the root cause untouched. Until you fix the core issue, the exact same problem is bound to return. [learn more](GST321_U1_T8#GST321_U1_T8_h4)

question: Staff nurses complain of severe exhaustion. Instead of just adding extra shifts, the manager investigates and discovers that broken equipment is causing major delays. What has the manager found?

options.B: The root cause of the exhaustion
options.D: The personal fault of the junior nurses

explanation: Brilliant! By looking past the surface complaints, the manager found the true source of the trouble. [learn more](GST321_U1_T8#GST321_U1_T8_h4)

question: Which of these is a real-world factor that often shapes a healthcare manager's choices?

options.A: The color scheme of the hospital exterior
options.B: The weather forecast for the upcoming weekend
options.C: The astrological sign of the nurse manager

explanation: What you have in terms of money, supplies, and available staff directly dictates what practical choices you can make. [learn more](GST321_U1_T8#GST321_U1_T8_h5)

question: Why might a nurse manager sometimes fail to use the most theoretically perfect solution to a problem?

options.A: Theory never has any connection to real-world nursing
options.B: Hospital policy forbids the use of logic in management
options.C: Staff members always refuse to do any work at all
options.D: Power dynamics and institutional policies create practical limits

explanation: In the real hospital environment, politics, hospital policies, and power struggles often force managers to find practical compromises. [learn more](GST321_U1_T8#GST321_U1_T8_h5)

question: What do we mean by 'confirmation bias' when a manager is making decisions?

options.A: Relying solely on the very first piece of news heard
options.B: Always asking senior doctors to make every choice
options.C: Noticing only data that supports preexisting beliefs
options.D: Refusing to make any choices without written permission

explanation: Confirmation bias happens when we accidentally ignore facts that contradict our ideas and only look for evidence that proves us right. [learn more](GST321_U1_T8#GST321_U1_T8_h6)

question: How can a nurse manager protect their decision-making process from personal mental biases?

options.A: Make all important administrative choices in absolute secrecy
options.B: Avoid gathering any data to keep the mind completely clear
options.C: Actively consult diverse team members and check objective data
options.D: Trust gut feelings completely without listening to anyone else

explanation: Getting input from your team and looking at hard facts is the best way to burst through personal blind spots! [learn more](GST321_U1_T8#GST321_U1_T8_h6)

question: What is key to getting staff members to gladly accept a newly introduced management decision?

options.A: Immediate disciplinary action for anyone who asks questions
options.B: Clear communication of the reasons behind the change
options.C: Changing the shift roster every single day without notice
options.D: Keeping all details of the new policy hidden from view

explanation: When nurses understand the 'why' behind a new policy, they are far more likely to support it and work together. [learn more](GST321_U1_T8#GST321_U1_T8_h7)

question: What should a nurse manager do if they check the results and realize a new decision isn't working out?

options.A: Permanently stop evaluating all ward outcomes
options.B: Ignore the data and pretend everything is fine
options.C: Tweak the approach or pivot to a new strategy
options.D: Blame the junior nursing staff for sabotage

explanation: Evaluation is there to guide you. If a strategy falls short, a great leader adjusts their sails rather than ignoring reality. [learn more](GST321_U1_T8#GST321_U1_T8_h7)
